- If sentiment shows strong bullish (e.g., 1.00) in recent days, model tends to overestimate and overshoot — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment shows strong bearish (e.g., -1.00) or mixed negative signals, model often underestimates — adjust downward bias, especially if recent price is rising.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >70), model frequently overreacts with continued steep upward trend — apply a “cooling-off” decay to forecast slope.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.00/0.25), model often fails to capture mean reversion — add a slight downward bias or momentum dampener.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion after a spike (e.g., 76→70), model tends to hold upward trend — force a correction toward historical mean or recent 10-day average.
- Forecast horizon 30d is prone to lagging sentiment shifts — if sentiment turns negative within 5 days, adjust forecast to reflect early reversal.
- If sentiment is positive but price is falling (e.g., 0.50 with downtrend), model often ignores trend — reduce forecast slope or add downward momentum filter.
- Model consistently overestimates in early days of a new 30d forecast — apply a “first-day discount” or reduce initial forecast by 5–10% if sentiment is neutral or bearish.
